hints: Focus on the type of bonding in copper and remember it is a metal with a giant lattice, not simple molecules.
Recall that in a metal the atoms lose valence electrons to become positive ions sitting in a sea of delocalised electrons.
Connect the high melting point to the large amount of energy needed to overcome the attraction between those oppositely charged particles.
walkthrough:
**Recall the structure of copper**

Copper is a metal, so it has a giant metallic lattice. It does not exist as separate atoms in the solid.

Lattice picture:
$$\text{Cu}^{+} \text{ ions in a sea of delocalised } e^{-}$$

**Describe metallic bonding correctly**

Each copper atom contributes its outer electron(s) to a mobile sea. What is left is a positive copper ion.
The bonding is the strong electrostatic attraction between the positive ions and the negative delocalised electrons.

**Link bonding to melting point**

Melting means loosening this lattice so particles can move. Because the ion to electron attraction is very strong, a lot of thermal energy is needed. That is why copper has a high melting point.

options.A: Incorrect. Copper in the solid is not made of neutral atoms only. The valence electrons are delocalised, leaving positive ions, so describing attraction between atoms only misses the real metallic bond.
options.B: Correct. Metallic bonding in copper is the strong electrostatic attraction between positive copper ions and the sea of delocalised electrons. Breaking this strong attraction requires a lot of energy, giving a high melting point.
options.C: Incorrect. Positive ions on their own would repel each other, not attract. The strong attraction only makes sense when the negatively charged delocalised electrons are included between the ions.
options.D: Incorrect. This mixes up the particles. The lattice contains copper ions, not neutral copper atoms, attracted to the delocalised electrons. Saying atoms is a common slip.
